archetype.name: Retooling (new staff, star QB sidelined)
archetype.definition: A first-year Jesse Minter team whose middling efficiency was masked by a soft early schedule and Lamar Jackson, now playing out a season with a backup quarterback, a leaky line and a division it can't catch.

report.headline: A fast start buried under a quarterback carousel and leaky protection
report.take:
This Ravens team is not what the early weeks suggested. The 41-23 opener at Indianapolis, with 324 passing yards and 202 rushing yards, looked like the 2024 machine that ranked first in offensive EPA. It wasn't. The wins that followed came against Tennessee, Atlanta and a Dallas defense that now ranks last, and once the schedule stiffened and Lamar Jackson started missing time, the Ravens stopped winning. They haven't won since mid-October. Minter inherits a roster that already slid in 2025, an 8-9 year with the defense 18th in EPA allowed. That is the same rank it holds now, so the defensive mediocrity isn't a new-coach dip. It carried over.

The record is honest. A -50 point differential implies 4.8 wins, and Wins Over Expected sits at -0.83, so the Ravens have been slightly unlucky, not lucky. The efficiency profile is a team in the bottom half almost everywhere it matters: 19th in offensive EPA, 21st in pass EPA, 18th in EPA allowed. Then there are quieter taxes. Special teams rank 27th in EPA per game, penalties 26th, and the line commits more penalties than all but three teams. The Ravens cover in only a quarter of their games because the Book keeps pricing them like the old Ravens.

The numbers also hide how much hinges on the passer. Five starts went to Jackson, four to Tyler Huntley and one to Joe Fagnano. Jackson's last start was a 91-yard, three-turnover mess at Buffalo, and he is now on injured reserve after thumb surgery, with a 6-to-10-week estimate. Behind a line that allows pressure at the fourth-worst rate in the league, Huntley can move the ball. He threw for 340 yards against the Chargers. But the run game vanished that night with 16 yards, while a Chargers offense ranked 32nd ran for 160 against this defense. The offense stays on schedule better than its EPA suggests, 13th in success rate. It just doesn't finish, and the defense bleeds deep.

From here the season is about pride and evaluation. Cincinnati, Pittsburgh and Cleveland all sit well ahead, and four of the last six games are division games. Jackson's estimated return lands in late December, too late to matter much. Expect a competitive but limited team that wins the games where Derrick Henry gets going and the turnover count stays low, and loses most of the rest.

strengths.title: Underneath defense that holds firm
strengths.body: Short passes and runs rarely hurt this defense. It ranks sixth in EPA on short throws, fifth in explosive run rate allowed and fourth in rushing touchdowns allowed per game. The front and the linebackers tackle well enough to keep everything in front of them, and that structural trait should hold even without Madubuike for stretches.

strengths.title: Henry still gets downhill
strengths.body: Derrick Henry has 185 carries, and the line opens enough room for 4.4 yards a carry, seventh in the league, with 2.6 yards before contact. The run game is the offense's identity with a backup quarterback. It peaks in games like Atlanta, where the Ravens ran for 208 yards. The yards are real, but the efficiency is only average, and the Chargers game showed it can disappear when the script turns.

strengths.title: Stays on schedule, plays aggressive
strengths.body: The offense ranks 13th in success rate despite its 19th-ranked EPA, so it moves the chains more consistently than it creates big plays. Minter's staff has gone for it on every fourth-down opportunity counted, first in the league. That combination keeps a Huntley-led team in games, as the one-score losses to Cleveland and the Chargers showed.

concerns.title: Quarterback carousel, Jackson out until late December
concerns.body: Three quarterbacks have started, and the passing game ranks 21st in EPA. Jackson's thumb surgery carries a 6-to-10-week estimate and a late-December return target. Huntley is a functional fill-in who can rack up yardage, but he doesn't threaten the defense the way Jackson does, and the offense loses its ceiling. This is the defining fact of the rest of the season.

concerns.title: Protection and line discipline
concerns.body: The line allows pressure on 24.5% of dropbacks, 29th in the league, and ranks 29th in line penalties per game. It also converts the lowest share of short-yardage runs in the league. This is a real flaw rather than a cost of style, and it compounds the quarterback problem, because a backup under pressure is where the 13 turnovers come from.

concerns.title: Deep shots and the opponent's WR1
concerns.body: The flip side of the tight underneath coverage is a secondary that gets beaten over the top. It ranks 27th in deep-pass EPA allowed, and the opponent's top receiver produces 0.72 EPA per target, second-worst in the league. With safety Jaylinn Hawkins out, the back end is thinner, so expect this leak to persist.

trend.note: Wins piled up through Week 5 against soft opponents. Every game since has been a loss, including back-to-back three-turnover blowouts at Buffalo and against Jacksonville, and then a home loss to the league's worst-ranked offense.

nextGame.headline: Two flawed teams; Carolina's missing pass rush is Baltimore's opening
nextGame.body:
Carolina is a mirror image in some ways. Its offense is better, 13th in EPA and 11th in scoring, and it leans on the pass, fourth in pass rate over expected. Its defense can't get home: 31st in sacks and last in sack rate and QB hit rate. That is the best news a line ranked 29th in pressure allowed could get, and it should give Huntley clean pockets. The catch is that Carolina takes the ball away, fifth in takeaways, and allows the second-lowest explosive pass rate. Huntley's path is a patient one through Henry, Mark Andrews and the backs, where Carolina ranks 27th against both the lead tight end and the lead back. The Book has Carolina -2.5 with a 43.5 total, and the Ravens pay +114.

Availability tilts things a little toward Baltimore's offense. Carolina will be without linebacker Bobby Okereke (89% snaps) and cornerback Will Lee III (73%), and fellow corner Mike Jackson is on injured reserve. A missing linebacker matters most against a Henry-and-Andrews plan. On Baltimore's side, Jackson is on IR, so Huntley starts. Safety Jaylinn Hawkins is out, a real problem against a pass-first opponent. Nnamdi Madubuike (hamstring) and guard Olaivavega Ioane (shoulder) are both questionable after leaving Monday's game, and losing Ioane would make the line problem worse.

waysToWin.title: Henry and Andrews at the soft spots
waysToWin.body: Carolina gives up more than usual to the lead back and the lead tight end, and it is missing Okereke in the middle. A run-heavy plan with play-action to Andrews plays to the Ravens' strengths and keeps a backup quarterback out of obvious passing downs. It also drains the clock from a Carolina offense that ranks 27th in time of possession.

waysToWin.title: Clean pockets and third-down conversions
waysToWin.body: Carolina's pass rush is the league's weakest by sack rate, and it allows conversions on 47.7% of third downs, 31st. If Huntley gets time and the Ravens stay on schedule, as their 13th-ranked success rate says they can, drives should finish. Carolina's red-zone defense ranks 29th.

waysToWin.title: Harass Bryce Young behind a leaky line
waysToWin.body: Carolina's line allows pressure at the third-worst rate. The Ravens' defense ranks 10th in QB hit rate even with a middling sack total. Getting Young off his spot before deep routes develop is the best cover for a thin secondary.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers feed a ball-hawking defense
waysToLose.body: The Ravens have 13 turnovers to 9 takeaways, and Carolina ranks fifth in takeaways with a turnover margin in the top third. The two three-turnover games in Weeks 8 and 9 were both blowouts, and Huntley forcing throws to chase points is the most likely way this one gets away.

waysToLose.title: Deep shots against a short-handed secondary
waysToLose.body: Carolina throws more than situations call for. The Ravens rank 27th in deep-pass EPA allowed and are without Hawkins. A couple of chunk plays to Carolina's top receiver would erase whatever the Ravens' ground game builds.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden-yardage battle
waysToLose.body: Special teams rank 27th in EPA per game and the Ravens are among the most penalized teams. In a game priced at under a field goal, a shanked punt or a drive-killing holding call can decide it, much as it did in the three-point losses to Cleveland and the Chargers.

nextGame.watch: Henry's early carries: if the Ravens run efficiently at a Carolina front missing Okereke, Huntley plays from comfortable downs against the league's weakest pass rush. If they don't, the game falls on his arm.

restOfSeason.body:
With Huntley under center until at least late December, the offense keeps its floor, thanks to Henry and a solid success rate, but loses its ceiling. The defense has been the same 18th-ranked unit for two seasons, so don't expect a second-half surge on that side. The record isn't hiding luck: the point differential implies almost exactly the wins they have. The next two games, at Houston and home to Tampa Bay, are the winnable stretch, though Tampa's defense ranks second. The finish is four division games against teams with winning records, including two against Pittsburgh and a trip to Cincinnati.

What could improve is the turnover margin and the special-teams tax, both of which tend to drift back toward average. What won't improve without Jackson is pass protection and the deep secondary. A Jackson return for the last week or two makes the finale more interesting but not the season. Realistically this is a six-to-eight-win team playing for draft position and for evaluating Minter's first staff.
swingFactors: Timing of Lamar Jackson's return from thumb surgery
Health of Madubuike and the interior line

confidence.note: Ten games and an honest point differential, but a quarterback split makes the season-long numbers a blend of two different offenses.
